Foreign Minister Petr Macinka accused the organizers of turning demonstrations into a business model.

Under the plan, public broadcasters would be funded from the state budget rather than through fees. The government argues that editorial independence will not be affected and that broadcasters need to cut costs. The suggested reform would reduce public media’s budget by 15 percent, and critics say the government wants more influence over the outlets.

Since the plan was introduced in April, several large protests have taken place, and Czech TV and radio held a one-day strike against it. The European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists and Reporters Without Borders have all criticized the proposal.

The governing coalition consists of Babis’s ANO party, the far-right SPD and the Eurosceptic Motorists. Polls show ANO still has around 30 percent support, even as the protests targeted the coalition. According to the Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026, trust in media in Czechia is low, at 30 to 33 percent, though public broadcasters are still regarded as “the most trusted brands.”
items.cav: The protester and organizer figures are unverified claims, and the sources do not give an independent count. The claim that the government seeks control of public media is the view of critics and protesters, while the government denies it.
items.op: Funding public broadcasters from the state budget may be defensible on cost grounds, but it hands ministers a lever over the newsroom. Before any cut takes effect, the government should show in public how editorial independence will be protected.

items.t: Spain and England meet in Madrid with top spot in Nations League Group A at stake
items.s: England and Spain meet in Madrid in the final group game of the UEFA Nations League, with both sides already through to the quarter-finals. The Guardian’s live coverage gives the lineups and Thomas Tuchel’s pre-match comments.
p: The match is scheduled to kick off at 7.45pm GMT in Madrid. Both teams have already qualified for the last eight, so the contest is about who finishes first in the group. According to the Guardian’s live blog, the group winner will face an unseeded side in the quarter-finals, with the second leg played at home. The competition resumes at the end of March.

Tuchel told ITV that “it’s a beautiful match”, and the Guardian’s preview argues that England have a good chance because of how Spain have set up. Spain are without Rodri, and Pedri is not in the squad, with Mikel Merino coming in for Fermín López. Lamine Yamal returns after being rested for the 2-0 win away to Czechia, and Oyarzabal starts as the centre-forward.

Spain are set to line up in a 4-3-3 with Unai Simon in goal, Marc Pubill, Cubarsi, Aymeric Laporte and Cucurella in defence, and Zubimendi, Fabián Ruiz and Merino in midfield. Pedro Porro, important at the World Cup, drops out. England pick a 4-2-3-1 with Jordan Pickford replaced by Trafford in goal, and a Konsa and Quansah centre-back pairing. Dan Burn is left out, Ben White starts at right-back, and Lewis Hall plays at left-back. Declan Rice and Elliot Anderson form the double pivot, with Kane leading the line.

The Guardian’s preview points to Kane dropping deep and Gordon and Rogers attacking the space behind Spain’s high line. The writer expects Spain to try to pull England’s midfielders wide, which the England side must avoid doing. The preview also says Spain’s defence was exposed at Wembley, where Spain won 3-2 and Harry Kane missed a penalty that would have made it 3-1 to England.

The fixture comes after England’s defeat in the World Cup semi-final, which the Guardian’s writer describes as a painful failure. That loss, and England’s earlier defeat in the Euro final, are used as reasons to ask whether the team can impose its own game rather than wait for the match to end.

Al Jazeera also has a live page for the fixture, but the material available to us for that outlet consists only of a summary and team-news headline, so its account of the match adds little beyond confirming the fixture and its status as the final group game.
items.cav: Most of the detail comes from a Guardian live-blog preview that mixes reporting with the writer’s opinion, so the tactical predictions are the author’s expectations, not confirmed plans. The Al Jazeera pages offered only short summaries, and no final score or result is available in these sources.
items.op: England’s tournament record should not be reduced to a single result, but the pattern the Guardian describes deserves scrutiny. Tuchel’s side must show it can play its own game rather than retreat, and the accountability for that choice belongs in public view.

items.t: Estonia to close all Russian border crossings after foiled drone factory arson plot
items.s: Estonia says it foiled an attempted Russian arson attack on a drone factory and will shut every border crossing with Russia by December 1. Prime Minister Karsten Michal blamed Russia’s GRU intelligence service.
p: Estonian authorities said on Sunday that they had stopped an attempted arson attack on a drone factory run by the defence company Threod Systems in Viimsi. Prime Minister Karsten Michal said the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence service, was behind the attempt, which he said took place on Saturday night.

Michal said “extensive damage” had been averted after law enforcement responded and detained the suspected attackers. He described the episode as part of a wider Russian hybrid war against Europe, aimed at reducing support for Ukraine.

Hours later, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Estonia would close all border crossings with Russia by December 1. He wrote on social media that hostile actions would not go unanswered and that the closure would limit Russia’s ability to carry out hostile activity and help prevent sanctions circumvention.

Tsahkna said he had informed the foreign ministers of Finland, Latvia and Lithuania. Estonia has several crossings with Russia and had until now been one of the few European Union states to keep them open.

The sources do not give details of the suspects’ identities, any charges, or the evidence linking the GRU to the plot. The attribution comes from the Estonian government and has not been independently confirmed.
items.cav: The Russian link is the Estonian government’s claim and is not independently verified. Reports differ on whether the factory was set alight or the arson was foiled, and the sources give no detail on the suspects.
items.op: Closing a border is a blunt instrument, and it lands on ordinary travellers and businesses who had nothing to do with the plot. If Tallinn wants the public to accept such costs, it should publish the evidence tying the GRU to the attack. Security measures need the same transparency as the threat they answer.

items.t: Canary Islands take roughly 1,500 arrivals in a single day, with El Hierro absorbing most of them
items.s: Roughly 1,500 to 1,600 people reached Spain’s Canary Islands on Saturday, most of them at El Hierro, according to figures reported by different outlets. The surge follows a larger crisis in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.
p: Spanish news agency EFE reported on Sunday, using tallies from the Spanish government’s maritime rescue body, that 1,580 people had arrived on Saturday. Most of them were brought to El Hierro, the smallest of the main islands in the archipelago’s western group, in 15 open wooden vessels. DW put the total for Friday and Saturday combined at more than 2,300.

Al Jazeera cited the Spanish rescue service with a lower figure for Saturday: 1,488 people taken from 14 dinghies, known as pirogues. It said that daily total exceeded a previous record of 1,461 set in November 2020. Al Jazeera also reported that more than 9,000 people have arrived in the territory since the start of November, and that Spain has declared a migration emergency there.

Most of those arriving departed from West African coasts, including Senegal, Gambia and Guinea. DW said the largest share came from those countries. Al Jazeera reported that one boat on Saturday carried 240 people, among them 12 women and 36 children, and that the International Organization for Migration had recorded at least 450 deaths on the Western African Atlantic route in the first ten months of the year.

Spain’s Territorial Policy Minister, Angel Victor Torres Perez, visited La Restinga, a town at the southern tip of El Hierro, on Sunday. She thanked residents for their solidarity and commitment. In a post on X, she said the government intends to handle the surge with humanity and with the island’s residents in mind. El Hierro has a population of nearly 12,000.

DW noted that overall migration to the islands fell 5.5 per cent between January and October 31 compared with the same period last year, so the recent spike is a sharp reversal within a broader decline. The surge also follows the events in late July, when an estimated 80,000 people, mostly young Moroccan men, crossed from Morocco into Ceuta. Al Jazeera reported that at least 100 people died during that crossing and that Spain deported more than a dozen of those who entered.

Al Jazeera said the European Union’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum took effect on June 12, 2026, and that the new rules have not stopped the flow of migrants to Spain. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has faced opposition criticism over his handling of Ceuta, and migration and housing are expected to be major issues for voters ahead of snap elections later this month.
items.cav: The sources give different figures for Saturday’s arrivals (1,580 in EFE’s tally as reported by DW, 1,488 in the rescue service figures reported by Al Jazeera) and do not explain the gap. The “more than 9,000” total and the record claim come from Al Jazeera alone, and the record’s comparison period is not detailed beyond the 2020 figure.
items.op: Numbers this large are easily reduced to statistics, yet each boat carries people who face real risk at sea. Spain’s government should publish consistent arrival and rescue counts, and explain its reception and deportation procedures in public. Emergency measures that lack transparency erode the public trust they depend on.

items.t: Estonia to close all Russian border crossings after alleged GRU-ordered attack on drone maker
items.s: Estonia will shut all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December, its foreign minister said, after eight people were detained over an attempted attack on a defence company that Tallinn blames on Russian military intelligence. The Kremlin has not commented on this case.
p: The Estonian government says Russia’s GRU military intelligence service ordered an attempted attack on Threod Systems, a Tallinn-area defence company that makes long-range attack and reconnaissance drones. Authorities said the aim was to cause an explosion and set the building on fire. The attack was reported to have taken place on Saturday, with eight people detained. No injuries or damage were reported by the company’s security team, though the prime minister said wider damage had been averted thanks to heightened security and a fast police response.

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna announced on Sunday, on X, that all Estonian-Russian border crossing points would close from 1 December. He cited what he called “clear evidence” of the GRU’s role, although the sources do not show that evidence. Estonia has three open crossings with Russia, at Narva, Koidula and Luhamaa. Authorities have not said how long the closure will last.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the closure was meant to reduce the risk of further attacks and to signal that assaults on the country’s defence industry would not be tolerated. He tied the incidents to Estonia’s support for Ukraine, arguing that Moscow wants Tallinn to become fearful and to weaken that backing. The government says it will tighten security and work more closely with businesses and allies.

Chief prosecutor Astrid Asi told reporters that the eight suspects live in Latvia. Al Jazeera, citing Latvian officials, described the arrests as involving “Latvian citizens and non-citizens”, which is a slightly different description. Estonia’s internal security service, Kapo, has asked a court to keep five of those detained in custody. The suspects have not been tried, and their guilt has not been established.

This is the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence firm that authorities have linked to Russia. An arson attack at Milrem Robotics in August was described by Kapo in September as a deliberate, pre-planned operation carried out for Russian special services. At that time Estonia summoned Russia’s chargé d’affaires, and the Kremlin rejected the accusation as baseless. Moscow has not yet responded publicly to the latest claims.

European intelligence agencies have warned for some time about sabotage against defence firms and Russian efforts to recruit people online for such acts. Mihkelson, chairman of the Estonian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, said the arrests showed the country could respond quickly, but argued that diplomatic protests alone were not enough.
items.cav: The sources do not publish the evidence behind the GRU attribution, and the Kremlin’s response to this specific incident is not yet known. Accounts differ on the timing (Saturday morning or night) and on the detainees’ nationality, and the damage reports vary between outlets.
items.op: Blaming Moscow may be justified, but closing every crossing is a blunt tool that also hits ordinary travellers and trade. Estonia should publish the evidence behind its attribution so that a measure this sweeping rests on proof the public can examine.

items.t: Hundreds of thousands rally in Prague against plan to fund Czech public media from the state budget
items.s: Organisers said more than 350,000 people joined a Sunday rally in Prague against a government plan to scrap licence fees for public broadcasters. Critics say the change would give ministers more influence over newsrooms.
p: Hundreds of thousands of Czechs gathered in Prague on Sunday to protest against a plan by Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’s government to end the mandatory licence fees that fund Czech Television and Czech Radio. Organisers said more than 350,000 people attended, which they described as one of the largest demonstrations in the country’s history. Euronews, citing media reports, put the figure at 350,000 to 400,000.

The rally was held at Letná Plain, the site of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that ended more than four decades of communist rule. Many participants wore triangular paper hats resembling Večerníček, an animated bedtime-story character who has become a symbol of the movement. Banners included the slogan “We won’t give media away.”

The government wants to finance the two broadcasters from the state budget instead. Protesters argue this would give ministers more leverage over editorial decisions. Sources say the future state subsidy would be far below current licence-fee revenue. The proposed changes would cut state television and radio budgets by about 15 per cent, according to the Guardian.

The organising group, Million Moments for Democracy, said the authorities would now see the scale of opposition. Its lead organiser, Mikuláš Minář, said the event was “just a beginning.” In a statement, the group demanded that the government withdraw the plan and accused Babiš and his partners of treating democratic institutions as their own property.

Euronews reported that the protest was tied to a vote in the Chamber of Deputies on the amendment, which the group summarised with the slogan “Never again 4:36”. According to Euronews, the majority cut short the debate, leaving more than 60 opposition MPs unable to speak. The Guardian dates the first reading to late October, and Euronews to mid-October, so the sources differ on timing.

The European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute have criticised the plan. They compared it with moves in Slovakia and Hungary, where media independence has been weakened under populist governments.

Babiš, a billionaire who returned to power last year, said the protests were based on unfounded claims. In an opinion piece he wrote that the government would not interfere in editorial work. Euronews also reported that students, theatres, writers, athletes, churches and healthcare workers voiced support for public media. Police said the demonstration passed without incident until early evening.
items.cav: Crowd estimates differ: the Guardian cites organisers’ figure of more than 350,000, while Euronews reports 350,000 to 400,000 from media reports. The timing of the first parliamentary reading is also reported differently. The 15 per cent budget cut and the fee amounts come from the sources and were not independently verified.
items.op: Public broadcasters need funding that cannot be turned into a lever over what they report. Moving them onto the state budget, while the government controls the purse, invites exactly that pressure. Parliament should answer the protesters with open debate and a full hearing, not a rushed vote in the small hours.

items.t: Iran launches second drone attack on US base in Bahrain in three days
items.s: Iranian drones were aimed at a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, according to the Guardian and the BBC, in the second such attempt in three days. The strikes further undermine stalled efforts to end the wider conflict.
p: Blasts were heard over Bahrain on Sunday after Iranian drones were aimed at a US base on the island kingdom, according to the Guardian. It was the second such attack in three days, and Tehran framed it as retaliation for recent US strikes inside Iran. The Guardian also said the episode deepened fears of escalation just as talks between Tehran and Washington appear stuck.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said it sent six drones toward a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base, which the BBC spells al-Riffa. The IRGC described the move as a response to “hostile US actions”. Bahraini authorities said their air defences stopped the drones before they reached their targets, and the BBC reported that the country’s military said the drones were destroyed before they could achieve their aims.

One report said Bahrain issued two alerts about possible threats on Sunday, its first such warnings since September, as explosions rattled the capital, Manama. Sirens were heard across the country, and the interior ministry told residents to move to the nearest secure place.

Bahrain’s foreign ministry denounced the attacks as brutal and said it holds Iran entirely accountable for what follows. Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Qatar also condemned the strikes and voiced support for Bahrain.

The latest attack followed an earlier one on Friday. The IRGC said it had hit a US early warning radar, but the US military denied that and said it had shot down two one-way drones with no injuries or damage. Before that, US forces struck Iranian targets, including Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. US officials told CBS the strikes were limited and defensive, and were a response to Iranian fire at a US aircraft. Iran’s state news agency Irna reported explosions on the island.

Diplomacy looks stalled. The conflict began in February with joint US and Israeli attacks on Iran, and a preliminary agreement reached in June fell apart within weeks. According to the Guardian, Donald Trump has said Washington is no longer seeking a deal and has asked Vice-President JD Vance to focus on alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states. Vance had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Tehran was “not waiting for anyone”.

In the Strait of Hormuz, the IRGC claimed that two ships struck mines and that one oil supertanker carrying 2m barrels sank. There has been no immediate independent confirmation of that claim. The US military has said it cleared all mines from the main routes through the waterway.

In Yemen, Iran-aligned Houthi rebels pushed forward against pro-government forces in the south. The main government-backed force announced it was pulling back from the Bab el-Mandeb area to defend Aden. AFP, citing military and government sources, reported that a Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12.
items.cav: The IRGC’s claims about the drone attacks and the tanker sinking have not been independently verified, and the US military disputes some of them. The casualty figures in Yemen are second-hand, relayed by AFP from unnamed sources.
items.op: Drone strikes on a host nation and threats to shipping leave little room for deals made behind closed doors. Whoever is responsible for each attack, the public deserves verified accounts of what was fired, where and why. A policy that shifts from negotiation to retaliation without explanation is the costliest route for everyone in the Gulf.

items.t: Thousands rally in Prague against plan to fund Czech public media from state budget
items.s: Thousands of people gathered in central Prague on Sunday to oppose the Czech government's plan to end the licence fee and pay for public media from the state budget. The government says editorial independence will be preserved.
p: Demonstrators argue that the proposal could give politicians room to limit media freedom. The ruling coalition, made up of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties, counters that broadcasters must reduce their spending and that editorial decisions would remain unaffected.

Parliament approved the first reading of the bill late last month, and protests have continued since then. At present, Czech households pay 205 crowns ($9.44; £7.06) per month for television and radio services.

The Million Moments for Democracy association, which organised Sunday's march, put attendance at “roughly 400,000.” That number comes from the organisers, and the reporting does not include an independent count.

Milana Rudolfova, a 72-year-old pensioner, told Reuters that she regards Czech Television as a reliable source of truth. Some marchers wore paper hats folded from newspaper in honour of Vecernicek, the cartoon figure who has long presented the broadcaster's evening children's stories.

Prime Minister Andrej Babis, who was appointed in December 2025, has rejected the idea that his government wants to control public media. Speaking to the Czech News Agency, he argued that the current system is outdated and that many European countries are adopting similar models.

Several European states have already left the licence fee behind. France abolished it in 2022, and its public broadcasters are now financed partly through a share of VAT revenue. Norway ended its fee in 2020 and placed public broadcasting costs within the national budget.

Critics have drawn parallels with Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who exercised tight control over state media during his time in office. In June, Pavol Szalai of Reporters Without Borders said that attacks on both private and public outlets had become a defining feature of Babis's tenure.
items.cav: The attendance figure is the organisers' own estimate, and the Hungary comparison is made by unnamed critics. The sources do not explain how the new funding model would operate in practice.
items.op: Public broadcasting should not depend on a government's promises about how it will behave. If the Czech state takes over its funding, the law must set firm safeguards for editorial independence and make the terms of any budget decision public. Assurances from the prime minister are not enough.

items.t: Duffy blames prior presidents and Congress for nationwide flight stoppage; Van Hollen says funds were underused
items.s: The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed earlier administrations and a lack of congressional funding for the travel chaos after a four-hour nationwide flight stoppage. A Democratic senator argued the Trump administration has not properly spent money it already received.
p: Donald Trump’s administration on Sunday attributed the travel disruption that followed Friday’s four-hour nationwide flight stoppage to prior presidents and to insufficient congressional funding, according to The Guardian. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop led to the delay or cancellation of thousands of flights.

Speaking to CNN, Duffy said: “I take responsibility for what was given to me.” He had earlier said that routine but necessary maintenance, botched by a contractor, caused the stoppage. He argued that the $12.5bn Congress provided was limited in scope and not nearly enough. He said it could not pay for new telecom architecture, new air traffic software or new towers, and that the existing systems date back to the 1990s.

Democratic senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland rejected that argument. He told CNN that it was “really rich” for the secretary to blame Congress, which he said had given the administration what it requested. In his view, the administration has not properly invested all the funds already allocated for upgrades. He said that if more money is needed, the administration should come forward and justify it.

Trump, who waited until Sunday to comment on the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years, blamed the Biden administration in a Truth Social post. He wrote that the administration had “the knowledge and plan” for flight control systems and that Congress needed to provide the money. Duffy said Trump had been in constant behind-the-scenes contact and was fully tracking events, though the report does not independently confirm this.

On CBS News’ Face the Nation, Duffy said the FAA was investigating the root cause of the botched work, which involved replacing old copper telecommunication lines with fiber optic cables. He said similar work had been done “thousands of times” without problems. The contractor, L3Harris, is reportedly conducting diagnostic tests. Duffy repeated that there was no sign of a foreign cyberattack.

The union Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (Pass), which represents more than 11,000 FAA workers, said its technicians were not involved in the upgrades behind the stoppage. It said the issue was isolated to two contractor-owned and contractor-maintained routers, and that contractors have historically followed a protocol in which FAA employees conduct a risk assessment. Asked whether a risk assessment was carried out in this case, Duffy did not directly answer, saying only: “We do risk assessments on everything.”

Duffy also cited a Government Accountability Office report from September 2026 that called for modernizing air traffic control systems, and he rejected concerns that speed was being prioritised over cost and disruption. Pass has called for better staffing of certified technicians and for a fuller role for its members in the modernisation effort.
items.cav: The accounts conflict: Duffy says the work was done appropriately, while the union says its technicians were not involved and questions the usual risk-assessment protocol. The root cause is still under investigation, and the contractor’s diagnostics are only reportedly under way. Trump’s claimed involvement is based on Duffy’s account and is not independently confirmed.
items.op: Whoever is at fault, the public is entitled to a clear account of who approved the work, what risk checks were done, and how the funds were spent. Blame passed between administrations and Congress does not answer those questions. Transparency about the investigation should come before any further political argument.

items.t: Gulf states condemn Iranian drone attack on Bahrain as Hormuz tensions rise
items.s: Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Qatar have condemned an Iranian attack on Bahrain, which Bahraini authorities said was intercepted. The strike is the latest sign that a two-month lull in fighting may be ending.
p: Early on Sunday, Iran reportedly sent six drones toward a US air base in Bahrain, raising fears that full-scale fighting could resume. Bahraini authorities said they had stopped the incoming threat and destroyed the drones before impact, and gave no immediate account of any harm to property or people.

The island state, which is home to a major US naval command, issued public warnings and activated missile sirens before the strikes arrived. Residents, who were hit by the second attack since Friday, said they were unsettled to see the violence return. One local resident voiced hope that the earlier calm would hold.

Tehran said its target was a radar installation at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base and described the operation as a response to recent American military action. Washington had not yet commented on the Sunday attack, though it has previously said the first attempt on Friday caused no damage.

The Bahraini state news agency published reactions from several governments in the region. Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry called the Iranian strikes a breach of international law and of the duty of good neighbourly conduct, urging an end to them. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry cautioned that the attacks marked a hazardous escalation that could derail diplomacy aimed at calming the region.

The incident sits within a broader standoff. US forces have conducted limited strikes on Iranian naval positions along the southern coast and on Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, with the stated aim of protecting oil tankers using the waterway. Iran insists that vessels crossing the strait without its approval are striking mines and sinking, and says it regards them as lawful targets.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards asserted that a supertanker loaded with more than two million barrels of oil had sunk after hitting a mine in the strait, and that two other ships had struck its mines. No independent confirmation of the tanker claim is available. Earlier, the US military had said it had cleared mines from the main shipping lanes.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told a news conference in Tehran that Iran would continue to answer any military action by the United States or other countries. Asked whether the latest attacks marked a change of course as talks with Washington have stalled, he replied that Tehran was acting in its own security interests and would not be held back by others.

Separately, the Iran-backed Houthis are increasing pressure on government positions around Aden, Yemen’s interim capital. Saudi-backed government forces said they had pulled back from their Bab el-Mandeb offensive in order to concentrate on defending Aden.
items.cav: The sources do not say whether the drones caused any damage, and the tanker sinking is a Revolutionary Guards claim that has not been independently verified. One part of the reporting mentions a strike on Tehran, but the rest of the account describes strikes on Bahrain and Iranian coastal and naval sites, so the details of that strike are unclear.
items.op: Condemning an attack on a neighbouring state is right, but the principle of international law must apply to every side. US strikes on Iranian sites and Iranian claims about mines both need scrutiny. Claims that shape the war, including the tanker sinking, should be verified independently before they are repeated as fact.
